title: Iff-split of the Kleene theorem: regular languages and regexp languages coincide
intent: State the Kleene theorem as an inhabitation equivalence between "L is regular" and "there is a regexp for L", then close each direction by applying one named correctness lemma — dfa_to_re_correct (DFA to regexp) for the forward direction and re_to_dfa_correct (regexp to DFA) for the backward — so the iff adds nothing beyond pairing the two constructions.

parent.name: regularP
parent.statement:
Lemma regularP (char : finType) (L : lang char) :
  regular L <-T->  { e : regexp char | forall x, L x <-> x \in e}.

children.name: dfa_to_re_correct
children.closed_by: apply/idP/big_plusP reflection split; both branches by rewrite -L_R set_enum dfa_L

children.name: re_to_dfa_correct
children.statement: Lemma re_to_dfa_correct (r : regexp char) : dfa_lang (re_to_dfa r) =i r.

applicability.goal_shape: An inhabitation equivalence P <-T-> Q (the project's `iffT`, a two-field record of P -> Q and Q -> P) between two constructible statements — here `regular L` (`{ A : dfa | forall x, L x <-> x \in dfa_lang A }`) and `{ e : regexp char | forall x, L x <-> x \in e }` — where each direction is already a named lemma `construction_correct` stating a language equality closed by rewriting.
applicability.use_when: each direction of the equivalence is already proved as its own named correctness lemma (a construction and its inverse), so the split merely pairs them; the two halves are genuinely different constructions whose content lives in the lemmas, not in the glue.
applicability.avoid_when: one direction still needs real work that no lemma already proves (the split then leaves a goal with the full difficulty); the two sides are not constructible types (a plain Prop equivalence `A <-> B` is split with `split`/`constructor` on `iff`, not on an `iffT`); or the directions are not symmetric constructions, in which case a one-line glue with two rewrites will not close them.

consequences: Creates two obligations, the two directions of the equivalence, each discharged by a pre-existing named lemma; the split itself adds no content, so the whole proof is only as good as the two correctness lemmas. Failure modes: if a direction is not already a lemma, the split leaves a goal carrying the full difficulty; and `<-T->` is a Type-level `iffT` between constructible types, so a plain Prop `A <-> B` must be split with `split`/`constructor` on `iff` instead, or the split will not apply.
